overview.title: 1. Overview
overview.p1: The BioResonance platform is a research visualisation tool for studying the effects of applied electric fields on biological membranes using the Schwan single-shell dielectric model. It computes the transmembrane potential (Vm) induced by a uniform alternating electric field, the specific absorption rate (SAR) and steady-state temperature via the Pennes bioheat equation, and the resulting disruption ratio for each cell or pathogen type. Advanced controls include field-to-cell orientation (cos θ), blood perfusion rate (ωb), and Maxwell-Garnett effective medium correction for dense cell suspensions.
overview.p2: Two simulation modes are provided: Schwan/IRE mode for cancer vs. healthy cell targeting via transmembrane potential, and Resonance mode for bacterial/viral capsid or cell-wall disruption at MHz–GHz frequencies. Cancer cells, bacteria, and enveloped viruses each exhibit distinct characteristic frequencies (fc) set by their size and membrane capacitance, enabling frequency-selective targeting. Note on Tumour Treating Fields (TTFields): TTFields (Kirson et al. [2]) operate at ~1–2 V/cm at 100–300 kHz and disrupt mitosis via dielectrophoretic forces on the mitotic spindle — a sub-threshold mechanism that does not rely on Vm threshold crossing. This platform models the IRE/electroporation regime (200–10,000 V/cm), not the TTFields regime.
overview.disclaimer: This platform is intended for research visualisation only and does not constitute clinical guidance or a validated medical device. All biophysical parameters are approximate values derived from the bioelectromagnetics literature.

schwan.title: 2.1 Schwan Equation
schwan.p1: For a spherical cell modelled as a single-shell dielectric in a uniform AC electric field, the peak induced transmembrane potential is given by the Schwan equation. The cos θ factor accounts for the angle between the applied field and the cell's long axis: θ = 0° (field-aligned) yields maximum coupling; θ = 90° gives Vm = 0. Crucially, cos θ cancels exactly in the selectivity ratio Vm,T/Vm,H, so field orientation does not affect the Therapeutic Index — it scales both cells equally. The orientation slider in the Advanced panel rotates both cells simultaneously.
schwan.p2: The membrane time constant τ determines the characteristic frequency f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πτ), above which V<sub>m</sub> falls at −20 dB/decade. Cells with large radius R, high membrane permittivity ε<sub>r</sub>, or thin membrane d exhibit a larger C<sub>m</sub> and lower f<sub>c</sub>, making them preferentially disrupted at lower frequencies relative to smaller reference cells. The extracellular conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> is temperature-corrected at each simulation step: σ<sub>e</sub>(T) = σ<sub>e0</sub> × (1 + 0.02 × (T − 37°C)), which shifts τ and f<sub>c</sub> dynamically as the medium heats.
schwan.eqSub1: ω = 2πf    τ = R · C<sub>m</sub> · (2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>) / (2σ<sub>e</sub> · σ<sub>i</sub>)
schwan.eqSub3: cos θ = |cos(θ)| — field-to-cell-axis coupling factor; θ = 0° (field-aligned) → max V<sub>m</sub>; cancels in V<sub>m,T</sub>/V<sub>m,H</sub> selectivity ratio
schwan.eqNote: Tadej Kotnik & Damijan Miklavcic, Biophys. J. 79:670 (2000) [9]

params.note: θ = angle between field and cell axis; 0° = max coupling; cancels in selectivity ratio
Computed from C<sub>m</sub> and conductivities; temperature-corrected σ<sub>e</sub>(T) used
4.5 (RBC) to 25 (enveloped virus). Physical lipid bilayer ε<sub>r</sub> ≈ 2–5; protein channels raise the effective value.

thermal.title: 2.2 SAR & Pennes Bioheat Model
thermal.p1: Ohmic heating is modelled via the specific absorption rate (SAR). The internal field factor α = 3σ<sub>e</sub>/(2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>) is the exact DC Clausius-Mossotti solution for a conducting sphere in a uniform field (Foster & Schwan [5]). At frequencies above f<sub>c</sub>, the membrane capacitance shields the cell interior, so the displayed SAR is an upper bound that grows as f → f<sub>c</sub> from below.
thermal.p2: Steady-state temperature follows the Pennes bioheat equation [14] with two parallel cooling pathways: Newton surface cooling (λNewton = 0.02 s⁻¹, representing combined thermal diffusion and surface loss) and blood perfusion cooling (λperf = ωb × 63.9 / cp), where ωb [mL/(g·min)] is set in the Advanced panel. In vitro experiments with no blood supply use ωb = 0. The 63.9 factor combines blood density (1060 g/L), specific heat (3617 J/(kg·K)), and unit conversion to s⁻¹ per mL/(g·min). At steady state: Tss = 37 + SAReff / ((λNewton + λperf) × cp).
thermal.scope: Thermal model scope: The Newton cooling coefficient λNewton = 0.02 s⁻¹ (time constant τth ≈ 50 s) represents tissue-level lumped heat dissipation — appropriate for macroscopic electroporation applicators in perfused tissue. A free cell in solution has τth ≈ R²ρcp/κ ≈ 0.6 ms (R = 10 µm, κ ≈ 0.6 W/m·K), equilibrating with its medium in milliseconds. The temperature displayed reflects bulk medium heating, not local membrane temperature, which is relevant for comparing treatment protocols rather than single-pulse effects.
thermal.eqSar: SAR = σ<sub>i</sub> · α² · E² · w<sub>f</sub> / ρ
thermal.eqSarSub1: α = 3σ<sub>e</sub> / (2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>)   (DC internal field factor for sphere in medium)
thermal.eqSarSub2: w<sub>f</sub> = 0.5 (CW sinusoidal)  |  1.0 (pulsed bipolar square wave / H-FIRE)
thermal.eqTssSub1: SAR<sub>eff</sub> = SAR<sub>peak</sub> × dc    λ<sub>Newton</sub> = 0.02 s⁻¹ (surface / diffusion cooling)
thermal.eqTssSub2: λ<sub>perf</sub> = ω<sub>b</sub> × 63.9 / c<sub>p</sub>    ω<sub>b</sub> [mL/(g·min)] — blood perfusion rate (Advanced panel)
thermal.eqNote: Pennes bioheat equation: Harold H. Pennes, J. Appl. Physiol. 1:93 (1948) [14]  ·  SAR formulation: Kenneth R. Foster & Herman P. Schwan (1989) [5]

maxwell.title: 2.3 Effective Medium (Maxwell-Garnett)
maxwell.p1: At high cell packing densities φ (volume fraction of cells), neighbouring cells reduce the effective extracellular conductivity σe,eff experienced by each cell. This is captured by the Maxwell-Garnett mixing rule [15] for insulating spheres in a conducting medium — the DC limit applicable when cell membranes are capacitive (f ≪ fc):
maxwell.p2: The simulation applies this correction to σ<sub>e</sub> before computing τ, V<sub>m</sub>, and SAR, so all downstream outputs reflect the dense-suspension environment. φ = 0 corresponds to isolated cells in bulk medium (in vitro single-cell); φ ≈ 0.64–0.74 represents random close-packing of spheres (dense tissue). The Cell Packing slider is in the Advanced panel. For most in vitro well-plate experiments, φ ≈ 0.01–0.05 (sparse); tumour tissue can reach φ ≈ 0.6–0.8. Note: the Maxwell-Garnett DC formula is the appropriate limit here — the full Bruggeman or Bergman–Milton bounds apply at higher frequencies and are not implemented.
maxwell.eqSub1: φ — cell volume packing fraction (0 = isolated cells; ~0.64 = random close-packing)
maxwell.eqSub2: DC insulating-sphere limit; valid when f ≪ f<sub>c</sub> (membrane capacitively opaque)
maxwell.eqNote: James Clerk Maxwell Garnett, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 203:385 (1904) [15]

disruption.title: 2.4 Disruption Criterion (IRE)
disruption.p1: Membrane disruption (irreversible electroporation; Neumann et al. [7]; membrane deformation dynamics reviewed in Dimova et al. [6]) is initiated when the disruption ratio exceeds threshold for a sustained period. The pulse-envelope factor fpulse = 1 − exp(−tp/τ) captures the RC charging dynamics of the membrane during a rectangular pulse of width tp (Weaver & Chizmadzhev [3]): at tp ≫ τ (standard IRE with µs pulses), fpulse ≈ 1 and the listed Vm,threshold values apply directly. At tp ≪ τ (nsEP with 10 ns pulses), fpulse ≈ 0.07 for a hepatocyte — the effective threshold is ~14× higher, requiring proportionally greater field for disruption. CW mode sets fpulse = 1.
disruption.p2: Cancer cells exhibit lower Vm,threshold (~0.65–0.85 V) than healthy tissue (~1.0–1.1 V), creating a therapeutic window where tumour cell disruption occurs at sub-lethal field intensities for normal cells. For adenocarcinoma vs. hepatocyte in saline, maximum Vm selectivity ≈ RT/RH = 1.5× occurs at quasi-DC (f ≪ fc(T)); the Therapeutic Index (accounting for different lysis thresholds) reaches ~2.4× at quasi-DC. Selectivity decreases with increasing frequency as the larger target cell rolls off before the smaller healthy cell.
disruption.revEp: The Rev-EP window (50–85% disruption ratio) represents reversible electroporation: pores open transiently and re-seal after the field is removed. This is the drug/gene delivery regime — cells survive. The simulation shows this state with an amber indicator. Increasing the field or duration beyond the 85% threshold arms the irreversible lysis countdown.
disruption.eqSub1: f<sub>pulse</sub> = 1 − exp(−t<sub>p</sub> / τ)   (pulse-envelope charging factor; pulsed mode only; 1.0 for CW)
disruption.eqSub2: 8–50% → Nourishing: sub-threshold biomodulation window (Ca²⁺ / NO signalling; §2.9)
disruption.eqSub3: 50–85% → Rev-EP window: reversible electroporation — pores open transiently and re-seal
disruption.eqSub4: Simulation arms lysis countdown when Disruption Ratio > 85% of threshold
disruption.eqSub5: Lysis fires after protocol time: t<sub>lysis</sub> = N × t<sub>p</sub>/dc (pulsed) or 2.5 s (CW)
disruption.eqNote: James C. Weaver & Yuri A. Chizmadzhev, Bioelectrochem. Bioenerg. 41:135 (1996) [3]

resonance.title: 2.5 Acoustic / Mechanical Resonance — Virus & Bacteria
resonance.p1: For sub-micron targets (virions and bacteria), the Schwan model predicts reduced selectivity at quasi-DC because Vm ∝ R — small cells generate lower transmembrane voltage than large cells. The correct disruption mechanism at GHz frequencies is acoustic/mechanical resonance of the capsid protein shell or bacterial cell wall, modelled by a Lorentzian lineshape. Mammalian cells lack the rigid protein/peptidoglycan shell required for this resonance; their Schwan Vm rolls off above ~1 MHz and approaches zero at GHz frequencies, leaving healthy tissue unperturbed at pathogen-targeting frequencies.
resonance.rfBasis: Experimental basis: The fres values are derived from femtosecond pulsed laser (near-IR, ~800 nm) experiments in which acoustic capsid normal modes are excited via impulsive stimulated Raman scattering (Tsen et al. [10]) — not direct RF/microwave delivery. The Ethr values (V/cm) for RF excitation have no experimental validation and are theoretical extrapolations included as research targets. The physical coupling mechanism between an RF electromagnetic field and GHz acoustic capsid modes is not established in the literature. Direct microwave excitation at 10–12 GHz in bulk tissue faces a penetration depth of ~1–2 mm, making in vivo delivery an unsolved engineering challenge.
resonance.envelopedBasis: Enveloped virus note: The Tsen et al. [10] and Dykeman & Sankey [11] models were experimentally validated on non-enveloped icosahedral protein-capsid viruses (M13, TMV, CCMV). Influenza A and SARS-CoV-2 are lipid-enveloped RNA viruses — their envelope is a fluid lipid bilayer with no well-defined mechanical resonance (Q ≈ 1, highly damped). The fres, Q, and Ethr parameters for enveloped viruses in this table are theoretical extrapolations not supported by published experimental data, included as exploratory research targets.
resonance.bacteriaQ: Bacterial peptidoglycan Q-factor: The Dykeman & Sankey [11] atomistic models were computed for icosahedral protein-capsid viruses, not bacterial cell walls. Peptidoglycan is a cross-linked viscoelastic polymer mesh with substantially higher mechanical damping than a rigid protein shell. Published acoustic spectroscopy data for isolated E. coli sacculi suggest an effective Q in the range 2–5 at GHz frequencies, versus Q = 20–50 for protein-capsid viruses. The values Q = 4 (E. coli) and Q = 3 (MRSA) represent the upper end of this range; the true peak may be substantially broader — in the near-overdamped limit (Q ≈ 1–2), the concept of a sharp resonance frequency breaks down.
resonance.infoBox: Switch to Resonance mode in the Experiment Lab (mode toggle in the setup bar) when working with bacterial or viral targets. The platform auto-tunes frequency to fres and sets field to 50% of Ethr when a resonance-enabled preset is loaded.
resonance.eqMain: Disruption ratio = (E / E<sub>thr</sub>) × L(f, f<sub>res</sub>, Q)
resonance.eqSub2: f<sub>res</sub> ≈ v<sub>shell</sub> / (2R)  ·  v<sub>protein capsid</sub> ≈ 1000–1500 m/s · v<sub>peptidoglycan</sub> ≈ 800–1200 m/s
resonance.eqSub3: Q — mechanical quality factor (protein capsid Q ≈ 20–50; peptidoglycan Q ≈ 2–5)
resonance.eqNote: Shian-wen D. Tsen et al., J. Biomed. Sci. 19:62 (2012) [10]; Eric C. Dykeman & Otto F. Sankey, Phys. Rev. E 81:021918 (2010) [11]

rows.basis: Larger spike envelope lowers f<sub>res</sub>; [10] analogue
v<sub>wall</sub> ≈ 1000 m/s; gram-neg. peptidoglycan; Q 2–5 range [11]
Thick peptidoglycan (20 nm); v<sub>wall</sub> ≈ 1500 m/s; near overdamped limit
No rigid-shell resonance — Schwan V<sub>m</sub> → 0 at GHz (ωτ ≫ 1); unaffected at pathogen frequencies

nsep.title: 2.6 Nanosecond Pulsed EP (nsEP) — Reference Model
nsep.p1: Nanosecond pulsed electroporation (nsEP) uses DC rectangular pulses (not sinusoidal RF) applied from specialised pulsed-power generators. The membrane charges as a first-order RC step response: Vm,eff(tp) = 1.5 · E · R · cos θ × (1 − exp(−tp/τ)). At tp = 10 ns in saline: τE.coli ≈ 14 ns → factor ≈ 0.51; τhepatocyte ≈ 147 ns → factor ≈ 0.065. The quasi-DC Vm ratio of 0.10× (E. coli vs. hepatocyte) improves to ~0.78× — the small cell charges proportionally more per pulse than the large cell. The theoretical TI limit as tp → 0 remains below 1× because Vm,thr,bacteria > Vm,thr,hepatocyte (cell-wall reinforcement raises the lysis threshold).
nsep.scope: Simulation scope: The Experiment Lab simulates duty-cycled AC sinusoidal fields — the Schwan Vm(f) model is evaluated at the RF carrier frequency, which is the correct model for continuous-wave RF or pulse-modulated RF bursts. True nsEP (DC rectangular pulses, pulsed-power hardware) uses the step-response formula above. The Pulse Width slider in the lab controls lysis protocol timing and the SAR waveform factor (fpulse), not Vm per se. For dedicated nsEP modelling, use the DC step-response formula directly.
nsep.eqMain: V<sub>m,eff</sub>(t<sub>p</sub>) = 1.5 · E · R · cos θ × (1 − exp(−t<sub>p</sub> / τ))
nsep.eqNote: Michael Stacey et al. [8]; Karl H. Schoenbach, Stephen J. Beebe & Eric S. Buescher [12]

doubleshell.title: 2.7 Double-Shell Nuclear Envelope Model
doubleshell.p1: For mammalian nucleated cells, an optional double-shell model (Kotnik & Miklavcic 2006 [13]) adds the nuclear membrane as a second concentric dielectric shell. The nuclear membrane Vm is a two-pole bandpass function of frequency, with peak at fpeak = 1/(2π√(τout·τne)) — typically in the 0.87–2.1 MHz range for the presets in this library. Cancer cells have a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio, thinner nuclear envelopes, and lower nuclear Vm thresholds, creating an additional cancer-selectivity axis. Enable via the Shell Model toggle in the Field Control panel.
doubleshell.fpeak: fpeak approximation accuracy: The formula fpeak = 1/(2π√(τout·τne)) is the geometric mean of the two time constants, exact only when τout ≫ τne or vice versa. For intermediate ratios (0.1 < τout/τne < 10) — which includes all presets in this library — the true peak deviates by up to ±30%. Displayed fpeak values are estimates; consult the full two-pole transfer function (Kotnik & Miklavcic 2006, Eq. 12) for precise computation.
doubleshell.thinShell: Thin-shell approximation: The model assumes Rnuc ≪ R (dilute-nucleus limit). For the adenocarcinoma preset, Rnuc/R = 8/15 ≈ 0.53 — near the boundary of validity. At this N/C ratio, the sphere-in-infinite-medium assumption underestimates nuclear field concentration by ~15%. The model remains a useful qualitative predictor of bandpass frequency and cancer selectivity trends.
doubleshell.sigmaNote: σ<sub>ne</sub> is not stored or used in the simulation. The implementation operates in the thin-membrane capacitive limit (σ<sub>ne</sub> → 0), per Kotnik & Miklavcic (2006) Eq. (14). Including finite σ<sub>ne</sub> requires the full complex admittance transfer function and is left for future work.
doubleshell.eqMain: V<sub>m,nuc</sub>(f) = (1.5 · E · R<sub>nuc</sub> · cos θ · ω·τ<sub>out</sub>) / √[(1+(ωτ<sub>out</sub>)²) · (1+(ωτ<sub>ne</sub>)²)]
doubleshell.eqNote: Tadej Kotnik & Damijan Miklavcic, Biophys. J. 90:480 (2006) [13]

uncertainty.title: 2.8 Cytoplasm Conductivity (σ<sub>i</sub>) Uncertainty
uncertainty.p1: Cytoplasm conductivity σ<sub>i</sub> is the most influential uncertain parameter in the Schwan model: it controls both τ and the SAR internal field factor α, affecting V<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub>, temperature, and the Therapeutic Index simultaneously. Literature values span considerable ranges depending on measurement technique (impedance spectroscopy, patch-clamp, rotation assay), ionic composition, growth phase, and osmolarity.
uncertainty.p2: The simulation visualises σi uncertainty as shaded bands on the frequency response chart (healthy: cyan, target: red, 10% opacity each). The band bounds are ±20% for mammalian cells, ±35% for bacteria, and ±45% for viruses. The TI uncertainty range displayed in the Selectivity Panel computes worst-case Therapeutic Index bounds: TIlow applies maximum σi penalty for the target and minimum for healthy; TIhigh applies the inverse. These bounds represent the realistic spread of outcomes across the literature parameter ranges — not measurement error or model uncertainty per se.

biomodulation.title: 2.9 Sub-threshold Biomodulation
biomodulation.p1: At disruption ratios below the electroporation threshold (DR 8–50%), pulsed electric fields can stimulate biological responses without causing membrane lysis. The simulation designates this the Nourishing state — named for the biomodulatory effects observed experimentally at sub-threshold field intensities. Two primary mechanistic pathways are established:
biomodulation.p2: Ca²⁺ influx via mechanosensitive and voltage-gated channels: Sub-threshold pulsed fields activate PIEZO1 mechanosensitive channels and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (Lee et al. [17]), generating transient intracellular Ca²⁺ spikes without permanent membrane permeabilisation. Ca²⁺ is a universal second messenger mediating downstream effects including gene expression, cytoskeletal remodelling, and cell proliferation. The optimal DR window for Ca²⁺ stimulation is approximately 20–40% of the lysis threshold.
biomodulation.p3: Nitric oxide (NO) signalling: Sub-threshold electromagnetic fields transiently modulate NO production via calmodulin-dependent nitric oxide synthase (CaM-NOS), with effects on vasodilation, inflammation resolution, and cell growth (Pilla [16]). This is thought to be a downstream consequence of the Ca²⁺ influx rather than a direct electromagnetic-NO interaction.
biomodulation.p4: The Nourishing state is therefore not a threshold of damage but a biomodulation window with potential therapeutic applications (tissue repair, anti-inflammatory, angiogenesis stimulation) distinct from the electroporation and ablation regimes. The simulation indicates this state on the cell card indicator bar and in the cell state tooltip. Recommended protocol for biomodulation: pulsed mode, low duty cycle (dc ≈ 10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁴), frequency below fc of the target cell, with DR ≈ 20–40%.

impedance.title: 2.10 Impedance Feedback & Ion Release Model
impedance.p1: As cells lyse during an electroporation protocol, intracellular ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, ATP, and other solutes) are released into the extracellular medium. This ion flux progressively raises medium conductivity σ<sub>e</sub>, which lowers the cuvette's DC impedance Z = d/(σ<sub>e</sub>·A). Because the generator and its connecting cable have a finite source impedance R<sub>s</sub> (typically 50 Ω for coaxial RF systems), the cuvette and source resistance form a voltage divider: as Z falls, the fraction of generator voltage dropped across the cuvette drops with it. Without field correction, the delivered electric field can fall significantly below the set point — particularly at high lysis fractions in small-volume cuvettes — compromising the protocol and invalidating dose comparisons between sessions (Kotnik et al. [20]).
impedance.p2: The Instrument Panel (/instrument) models this drift in real time. The ion-release model computes the live conductivity from the current disruption ratio; the corrected generator output is then displayed so the operator knows exactly how much to increase the generator voltage to maintain a constant intra-cuvette field.
impedance.eqMain: σ<sub>e</sub>(t) = σ<sub>e₀</sub> + φ · f<sub>lysed</sub> · (σ<sub>i</sub> − σ<sub>e₀</sub>) · η
impedance.eqSub1: φ = N · (4/3)π R³  ·  cell volume fraction
impedance.eqSub2: f<sub>lysed</sub> = max(0, (DR − 0.85) / 0.15)  ·  fraction of cells past lysis threshold
impedance.eqSub3: η = 0.8  ·  ion-release efficiency (reduced by protein–polymer crowding in released cytoplasm)
impedance.eqZ: Z = d / (σ<sub>e</sub> · A)  ·  DC cuvette impedance [Ω]  ·  valid for f ≪ 340 MHz in saline
impedance.eqCorr: E<sub>gen</sub> = E<sub>target</sub> × (1 + R<sub>s</sub> / Z)  ·  corrected generator field [V/cm]
impedance.eqNote: Kotnik, Rems, Tarek & Miklavcic, Trends Biotechnol. 37:1229 (2019) [20]; cuvette DC model: standard electrochemistry
impedance.hardwareP: In the default Simulated mode the ion-release model drives the impedance display. To replace the simulation with real instrument data, connect an impedance analyser or LCR meter to the BioResonance backend socket and emit the impedanceReading event. The backend validates the packet and re-broadcasts impedanceBroadcast to all connected UI clients. Switch the Sensor Mode toggle to Live Hardware in the Hardware Input card to activate this override. The hardware Zreal replaces the simulated value; σe is back-derived as σ = d/(Zreal·A).
impedance.hardwareSchema:
Socket event: impedanceReading → backend → impedanceBroadcast
Required fields: zReal [Ω], zImag [Ω], freqHz [Hz], timestamp [Unix ms]
Optional: conductivity [S/m] (pre-computed σe from instrument)

sonification.title: 2.11 Auditory Display (Sonification)
sonification.p1: Sonification is the use of non-speech audio to convey information. In the context of this platform, live experiment parameters are mapped to audible tones via the Web Audio API, enabling an operator to monitor experiment state without continuously watching the screen — a technique first formalised by Kramer et al. (1999) [21]. The technique is particularly suited to multi-parameter monitoring during long electroporation protocols where both impedance drift and cell disruption ratio evolve simultaneously.
sonification.disclaimer: Important: These sounds are NOT the RF treatment frequencies. The electroporation and resonance frequencies used in this platform are in the kHz–GHz range — far above the 20 Hz–20 kHz audible spectrum. The sonification maps data values to audible tones; it has no physical relationship to the applied field and does not affect the cells.

mappings.note: Higher drift = higher pitch; maps absolute drift % logarithmically
Louder = higher DR; scales from 0% to 100% lysis
Amplitude modulation flags the reversible electroporation window
Single A5 tone marks the lysis threshold crossing

sonification.p2: The Auditory Display is enabled from the Instrument Panel via the ♪ button. The pitch bar below the button shows the current pitch frequency in real time. All mappings follow the design principles in Walker & Kramer (2006) [22]: pitch is an effective ordinal scale for scalar quantities; AM tremolo is a distinctive qualitative marker for state transitions; and the mapping direction (higher = more disrupted) is intuitive and consistent with spectral urgency conventions.
sonification.refNote: Kramer G. et al., Sonification Report: Status of the Field and Research Agenda. ICAD (1999) [21]  ·  Walker B.N. & Kramer G., Mappings and Metaphors in Auditory Displays. ACM Trans. Appl. Percept. 2006 [22]

s01.title: Select cell pair
s01.desc: In the Experiment Lab, use the preset picker in the setup bar to choose healthy reference and target cell types. Each preset loads biophysical parameters from the cell library (see Data Sets tab). Open the Cell Parameters panel on either card to enter custom values or perform sensitivity analysis. For bacteria and virus targets, the mode toggle automatically offers Resonance mode.

s02.title: Set propagation medium
s02.desc: Choose the extracellular medium (Saline, Blood, Tissue, or Water) using the radio pills in the Field Control panel. Medium conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> directly modifies τ for all cells, shifting f<sub>c</sub> markers on the chart and scaling V<sub>m</sub>. Physiological saline (σ<sub>e</sub> = 1.5 S/m) is the standard reference medium for in vitro experiments. For in vivo tissue modelling, select Tissue (σ<sub>e</sub> = 0.4 S/m) and enable blood perfusion via the Advanced panel.

s03.title: Configure advanced parameters
s03.desc: Open the Advanced panel to set: Cell Orientation θ (angle between field and cell axis — affects Vm amplitude but not selectivity ratio); Blood Perfusion ωb (0 for in vitro; 0.5–5 mL/(g·min) for tissue); Cell Packing φ (0 for isolated cells; up to 0.74 for dense tissue). These parameters update all computed values in real time.

s04.title: Establish baseline at sub-threshold field
s04.desc: Begin with the default field intensity (150 V/cm for cancer targets). Both cells should display disruption ratios well below 50%. Click Log Reading in the Experiment Log panel to record the baseline state. This first manual entry anchors the session dataset.

s05.title: Identify the optimal frequency window
s05.desc: Cancer targets (IRE / Schwan mode): The golden ⭐ marker shows the optimal broadcast frequency. For most cancer vs. normal cell pairs, selectivity is maximised in the quasi-DC regime (f ≪ fc(T)), where Vm selectivity = RT/RH. The fc markers show where each cell's Vm begins to roll off. Click ⭐ in the Selectivity Panel to snap to this frequency. Bacteria / virus targets (Resonance mode): Switch to Resonance mode. The platform auto-tunes frequency to fres. Tune frequency to the Lorentzian peak for maximum disruption.

s06.title: Increase field intensity toward target threshold
s06.desc: Raise the Field Intensity slider incrementally. Monitor the Target disruption ratio on the CellCard and Selectivity Panel progress bars. For adenocarcinoma vs. hepatocyte in saline at quasi-DC, lysis occurs near ~311 V/cm for the cancer cell while the healthy cell remains below 50% disruption. Field Sweep Analysis: Open the Field Sweep panel to visualise DRT and DRH across the full field range. The therapeutic window (green fill: DRT ≥ 85% and DRH < 50%) is highlighted automatically. Use the ⭐ Set to Window Center snap bar button to apply the window midpoint. Note: this sets the live field intensity to within the lysis zone — the cell card will arm the lysis countdown. Log readings at each significant threshold crossing.

s07.title: Record lysis event and review temperature
s07.desc: When target cell lysis occurs, an entry is automatically added to the Experiment Log with event type lysis. Check the temperature readout on both cell cards. If temperature approaches 42 °C, consider reducing field intensity, increasing blood perfusion ωb, or switching to a lower-conductivity medium to reduce SAR. For nsEP targeting, reduce duty cycle — SAReff = SARpeak × dc.

s08.title: Explore biomodulation window (optional)
s08.desc: For research into sub-threshold biomodulation, reduce field to achieve DR ≈ 20–40% of threshold (Nourishing state). This range activates PIEZO1 and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels without causing lysis. Use pulsed mode with low duty cycle (dc ≈ 10⁻⁴). Log readings to document the sub-threshold state in the session CSV.

s09.title: Change cell preset and repeat parametric study
s09.desc: Switch to a different target preset (e.g. GBM, MCF-7, E. coli) and repeat steps 4–7. Compare selectivity ratios, fc positions, and lysis thresholds across cell types. Use the Cell Parameters panel and σi uncertainty bands on the chart to assess sensitivity to parameter variability. Cell Population Model: Open the Population Model panel and set a radius variance (1–30%) to generate a Gaussian-sampled cell population (Box-Muller sampling, N = 100–1000 cells). The histogram shows the distribution of disruption ratios and the fraction of cells in each state (Lysed %, Rev-EP %, Nourishing %). This quantifies treatment efficacy across biological heterogeneity — critical for assessing whether all target cells are reached by a given protocol while healthy cells remain sub-threshold.

s10.title: Export session data for analysis
s10.desc: Navigate to the Reports tab to review the full session log. Edit the session name, then click Export CSV to download a structured file containing all logged parameters: frequency, field, Vm, selectivity ratio, disruption ratios, temperatures, and event type.

s11.title: Monitor and compensate impedance drift (Instrument Panel)
s11.desc:
Navigate to the Instrument tab. Verify the Cuvette Setup card matches your physical cuvette geometry (gap, cross-section, source impedance Rs). The Live Impedance Status card shows the simulated σe rise as cells lyse. The Field Correction card shows the corrected generator voltage needed to maintain constant intra-cuvette field.

To connect a lab instrument (hardware mode): Wire an impedance analyser or LCR meter to your measurement PC, run a bridge script that emits JSON to the BioResonance backend socket event impedanceReading, then switch the Sensor Mode toggle to Live Hardware. Required packet fields: zReal [Ω], zImag [Ω], freqHz [Hz], timestamp [Unix ms]. The backend validates and re-broadcasts to all UI clients. If the reading is older than 5 s, the status indicator turns amber (stale). A typical 1 mm BTX cuvette with 1× PBS starts at Z ≈ 165 Ω; at 100% lysis the impedance may drop 10–20%, requiring ~11–25% generator voltage increase.

s12.title: Enable auditory display for hands-free monitoring
s12.desc:
On the Instrument Panel, click the ♪ Auditory Display button to activate sonification. Impedance drift is mapped to pitch (220–1760 Hz); disruption ratio controls volume; the reversible-EP window triggers a 6 Hz tremolo; lysis events produce an 880 Hz burst.

Note: These tones are NOT the RF treatment frequencies — they are audible data representations only. Allow browser audio permission when prompted. The pitch bar below the button shows the current pitch in Hz and updates at 10 Hz. For noisy lab environments, use headphones. See §2.11 for the full parameter-to-sound mapping table and methodology references (Kramer et al. [21]; Walker & Kramer [22]).

safety.title: 4. Safety & Thresholds
safety.intro: The following reference thresholds are used in the simulation and are based on published bioelectromagnetics literature.

rows.sig: Electroporation threshold (pulsed µs); irreversible membrane disruption
Normal epithelial / hepatocyte threshold; 1.5× higher than cancer cells
Higher due to cell wall reinforcement (peptidoglycan); IRE TI vs. mammalian < 1
Pores open transiently and re-seal; drug/gene delivery regime. Target cells only.
Sub-threshold Ca²⁺ / NO signalling; optimal at DR ≈ 20–40% (see §2.9)
Sustained thermal damage onset (IAHT threshold). Lepock (2003) [18]
Collagen ~60 °C, albumin ~68 °C; reduce field / duty cycle immediately
Water boiling / steam pressure; instant cell destruction regardless of V<sub>m</sub>
Regulatory whole-body average SAR limit for MRI equipment; reference upper bound for pulsed RF
FCC/IEEE partial-body SAR limit (1 g tissue average)
Arms when DR > 85%; fires after N<sub>pulses</sub> complete cycles. Clamped to [0.2 s, 30 s]. N and t<sub>p</sub> set in Advanced panel.
Sub-ablative to ablative IRE range (Davalos et al. [4]). TTFields use ~1–3 V/cm — distinct non-V<sub>m</sub>-threshold mechanism not modelled here.
At GHz and >500 V/cm, use ultra-low duty cycle to prevent bulk heating. SAR model is an upper bound at f ≫ f<sub>c</sub>.
